info.bio:
Roxanne Shanté (born Lolita Shanté Gooden on November 9, 1969) is an American hip-hop pioneer. Born and raised in the Queensbridge Projects, Shanté first gained attention through the Roxanne Wars and her association with the legendary Juice Crew.

Shanté's career began at the age of 14 when she encountered influential record producer Marley Marl, radio DJ Mr. Magic, and Tyrone Williams talking about how UTFO had canceled their appearance at a show they were promoting.

scenes.name: Marley Marl y la Juice Crew
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Los noctámbulos del Disco Fever se bautizaron Juice Crew y Mr. Magic pasó a ser Sir Juice: el primer colectivo de estrellas, con la producción de Marley Marl. Becario de estudio en Queensbridge, Marley descubrió hacia 1985 que podía aislar el golpe de caja de un disco y tocar sus propios ritmos con un sampler: cambió el sonido del hip hop y, sampleando a James Brown («el primer b-boy»), abrió el camino a Pete Rock, DJ Premier, Large Professor o RZA. Cuando U.T.F.O. dejó plantado a Mr. Magic, Marley grabó con Lolita Gooden, de catorce años, «Roxanne’s Revenge», un ataque que desató docenas de respuestas y lanzó a Roxanne Shanté; siguieron MC Shan («Marley Marl Scratch», el inicio del boom bap), Craig G, Biz Markie, Big Daddy Kane, Kool G Rap y Masta Ace, casi todos en Cold Chillin’ (Fly Ty Williams y Len Fichtelberg), un sello que «robaba a sus artistas». «The Symphony» (1988), improvisada tras una sesión de fotos, con Ace, Craig G, G Rap (que rapeó hasta que se acabó la cinta) y Kane, fue uno de los primeros posse cuts. Queensbridge, el mayor complejo de vivienda pública del país, a un puente de Manhattan, dio también a Cormega, Havoc, Capone o Nas: «un gumbo de magnificencia», una Roma.

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …DJ Marley Marl (producer, Juice Crew): “Roxanne’s Revenge” was never supposed to be a record. That was my special version of “Roxanne, Roxanne.” Shanté was a girl rapper from the block. Her, [MC] Shan, and this guy named Infinite used to have all these battles on the block when I used to be coming home, and one day I stopped by. I was like, “Wow, that’s intense and shit.” Shanté, she was one of the best out there at that time. Now you guys [U.T.F.O.] are talking about trying to get Roxanne. I got the girl y’all trying to get.

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: …early “diss record,” a song that verbally attacks a target, quickly became a sensation, bringing immediate cachet to Gooden (who started going by “Roxanne Shanté”), Mr. Magic, and Marley Marl. Mr. Magic and Marley Marl spent the night, and I got up in the morning, came down, and they’re in my living room, on my couch, covered in blankets, eating cereal, watching cartoons. Lady B (artist, radio DJ, Philadelphia): Roxanne Shanté was like a little sister to me. [I] loved her to death. I also had relationships with all the ladies that were coming out with the Roxanne songs. I gave a fair spin to all of the Roxannes. I played Shanté, I played the Real Roxanne. It was a fun time, because it was all about the battling. MC Shan (Juice Crew, Queensbridge): We used to do it on the benches for fun, but then when I got on tour with Shanté and seen that I could make money, I’m not going back to work. mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: (DAVID CORIO/MICHAEL OCHS ARCHIVES/GETTY IMAGES) Philadelphia’s Pop Art Records released Roxanne Shanté’s “Roxanne’s Revenge” in 1984. The song spawned countless response records and established Shanté as one of hip-hop’s first female breakout stars.

mentions.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
mentions.author: Jonathan Abrams
mentions.text: (DAVID CORIO/REDFERNS) MC Shan was one of the earliest hip-hop artists hailing from Queensbridge, the public housing development that also produced Roxanne Shanté, Cormega, Nas, Mobb Deep’s Havoc, and many others.
